payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
There's a pattern showing up in the provenance-for-music space that's worth naming on its own. It isn't the detection critique. That's already been argued. This is something else, and it sits underneath the surface of several products now claiming to offer authorship verification for music.

The pattern looks like this. A vendor requires a government-issued ID before a creator can use the system. After the ID check, the vendor performs cryptographic operations on the audio file. A hash of the file's contents. A trusted timestamp recording when the hash was created. The whole package gets sold as "provenance for music."

The cryptographic operations are correct. The hash is a hash. The timestamp is a timestamp. Both operations would produce the same outputs whether the signer presented a passport or not.

That's where the conflation hides.

What the gate actually is

The government ID check is not a property of the cryptographic operation. It's a separate layer the vendor bolted on. The hash doesn't get stronger because the person hashing the file showed a driver's license. The timestamp doesn't carry more legal weight because it was preceded by a KYC step. The signature is the signature. The gate is something else.

When a vendor combines the two and sells the bundle as provenance, two things happen. The technical claim is correct: yes, the file is cryptographically signed. The institutional claim is misleading: no, the signature is not what's being gated. What's being gated is who's allowed to use the cryptographic primitives at all.

That's a permission system, not a proof system.

Open and gated produce the same outputs

Here's the part that gets overlooked. Open authorship provenance and gated authorship verification produce identical cryptographic outputs. The hash is the hash. The timestamp is the timestamp. A signature created by someone who walked through a KYC flow is mathematically indistinguishable from a signature created by someone who didn't.

What differs is the surrounding ecosystem. Who can participate. Who controls the entry point. Who collects rent at the gate. What happens if the gatekeeper revokes access. What happens if the identity provider gets compromised.

Those aren't cryptographic differences. They're structural ones. And they decide which kind of industry the technology actually builds.

Authorship doesn't ask for permission

Copyright in most jurisdictions attaches at the moment of creation. The songwriter writes the song. The right exists. No registration is required. No ID is required. The legal system long ago decided that authorship is an act, not a credential. Registration comes later, optionally, for enforcement purposes. The authorship is already real.

Cryptographic authorship works the same way. The signature is generated by the act of signing. The act doesn't require permission. The primitive doesn't care who you are or whether you've passed a KYC check.

Now imagine if a vendor proposed the following. From here on out, copyright will only attach to your work after you show a private company your government ID, pay them a monthly fee, and let them administer the moment of creation. The right itself wouldn't get stronger. A gate would get added.

That's the pattern showing up in music provenance. Open primitive. Closed permission. Sold as one product. The primitive does the persuasion work. The gate does the rent extraction.

Why this matters in music specifically

Music has a global creator base. A meaningful share of working artists do not have government-issued ID in the form a US-based vendor will accept. Many are independent. Many work across borders. Many release through tiny labels or directly. Requiring an institutional ID at the entry point doesn't filter for authenticity. It filters for paperwork.

A signature should attach to a work because the creator made it. Not because the creator passed a KYC check administered by a private vendor. The cryptographic operation doesn't require the gate. The vendor is adding it because the gate is the business model.

That's the move worth seeing clearly. Open primitives, gated participation, sold as one product.

The naming damage runs forward

There's a second-order problem worth flagging. When a vendor calls their gated package "provenance," every later system that tries to ship open provenance has to explain why theirs is the real one. The vocabulary gets occupied. Procurement teams hear "provenance" and assume KYC. Policy drafters write provenance into regulation with the gated version in mind. Standards conversations inherit the conflation.

This is how mature primitives get captured. Not by being broken. By being bundled with something else and renamed.

The fix is to keep the two operations separate when describing the work. Cryptographic signing is one operation. Identity verification is another. Either can be open or closed. Either can be paid or free. They don't have to ship together, and they don't have to be administered by the same party. Bundling them and renaming the bundle is a marketing choice, not a technical one.

Authorship provenance does not require a gatekeeper. The cryptographic primitives have never required one. Any product that adds one is doing something else and calling it provenance.

The gate is not the signature.
payload.title: The gate is not the signature
